method: Editorial formative checks; 10 checks for opening orientation and 2 for every subsequent question. Source passages control answers; stage 1 is recognition and stage 2 is discrimination, followed by guided explanation, reconstruction, evaluation and application at later levels.

questions.question: Which kind of knowledge has belief or assent as its end?
options: Knowledge of what action to perform
Knowledge of rules for deciding proofs
Knowledge concerning propositions to be believed
Knowledge of the qualifications of jurists
questions.explanation: In §2 Ibn Rushd first identifies knowledge whose end is belief, before describing practical and instrumental knowledge.

questions.question: What kind of knowledge concerns a ruling on a particular prayer?
options: Particular practical knowledge
Rules of correct inquiry
Universal theoretical knowledge
The qualifications of a mujtahid
questions.explanation: Prayer rulings are Ibn Rushd’s example of particular knowledge directed towards action.

questions.question: Which activity is closest to Ibn Rushd’s third kind of knowledge?
options: Learning the name of a prayer
Learning a general class of rulings
Memorising a specific fatwā
Determining when an indication genuinely proves something
questions.explanation: The third kind supplies rules and conditions by which the mind judges indications, not merely a practical conclusion.

questions.question: In the four-part arrangement, where are the proofs used to derive rulings examined?
options: Part I: rulings
Part III: methods of derivation
Part II: sources
Part IV: qualifications of the jurist
questions.explanation: §5 assigns evidential methods and their use to the third part; the fourth is about the competent jurist.

questions.question: What does the compass-and-straightedge example chiefly illustrate?
options: How tools substitute for every act of thought
Why all legal results are certain
How methodological rules check reasoning
Why legal cases must be measured physically
questions.explanation: §2 compares these instruments to rules that guard inquiry against error; it does not make every inference demonstratively certain.

questions.question: A scholar knows the general divisions of legal rulings. Does universality alone make this methodological knowledge?
options: Yes, because every universal proposition is a rule of inference
No, because its end can still be practical knowledge
Yes, because only particulars are practical
No, because rulings cannot be universal
questions.explanation: §§2 and 6 distinguish universal knowledge about rulings from knowledge of the procedures for deriving them.

questions.question: Why did formal rules become more necessary after the earliest generations?
options: The relevant reasoning capacity ceased to exist
The Qurʾān no longer counted as a source
All early legal opinions became invalid
The discipline grew complex amid dispersed and divergent transmission
questions.explanation: §3 cites increasing complexity, dispersal and differences in reports, not a loss of all earlier reasoning competence.

questions.question: What does Ibn Rushd claim about the Companions’ legal reasoning?
options: They used the capacity without studying it as a separate discipline
They never used rules of inference in any form
They all independently compiled full uṣūl manuals
They rejected examining evidence
questions.explanation: §4 explicitly distinguishes using the capacity from formally investigating a science bearing its name.

questions.question: What is the scope of §4's induction claim?
options: Every principle was deduced from one report
No universals can be drawn from individual fatwās
Many universal notions were inferred from case-by-case legal opinions
Individual opinions become infallible once collected
questions.explanation: Ibn Rushd says many universal notions were established inductively from early fatwās, not that all opinions or principles were certain.

questions.question: In §6, why is the third part the distinctive inquiry of uṣūl?
options: It lists the highest-ranked jurists
It examines the method used to derive rulings from sources
It simply catalogues particular acts
It establishes the history of textual transmission
questions.explanation: §6 identifies the third part’s concern with rules of derivation as distinct in kind from knowledge directed towards action.

questions.question: Which pair of rulings differs chiefly over threatened omission in §17?
options: Obligatory and recommended
Forbidden and disliked
Permissible and recommended
Valid and invalid
questions.explanation: Both obligation and recommendation favour doing the act; obligation includes a threat concerning unqualified omission.

questions.question: A child’s property is subject to a legal consequence, but the guardian must act. Which distinction explains this?
options: Source versus transmission
Proof versus report
Addressee versus what the ruling concerns
Analogy versus syllogism
questions.explanation: §36 distinguishes the addressee of a command from the act or thing to which its consequences relate.

questions.question: Which is an example of an obligation allowing a choice rather than demanding one determinate act?
options: One named prayer with no alternatives
An obligation satisfied by one of several specified acts
A forbidden act with an exception
A permission without any demand
questions.explanation: §18 distinguishes a determinate duty from a duty discharged by choosing an authorised alternative.

questions.question: A prayer may be performed early or later within its appointed period. What follows?
options: All performance within the period is merely recommended
The duty disappears when its earliest moment passes
Postponement equals resolving to omit prayer altogether
The duty remains, though the timing can be chosen within limits
questions.explanation: §§21–22 allow postponement within a defined window without converting the obligation into a recommendation.

questions.question: What two respects are distinguished in prayer on usurped land?
options: Language and translation
Performance of prayer and wrongful occupation
Consensus and report
Ablution and fasting
questions.explanation: §31 separates the commanded performance of prayer from the prohibited occupation of another’s land.

questions.question: If a prayer has legal validity, what does that by itself establish about wrongful occupation?
options: It is also obligatory
It is always excused
It is independently permitted
It does not make the separate wrong permissible
questions.explanation: Legal validity is a specific judgement about discharging a duty; it does not justify a different wrongful description.

questions.question: Who is the relevant addressee in the child’s-property case of §38?
options: The guardian responsible for the act
The property itself
The child as a fully responsible adult
The transmitter of the report
questions.explanation: Ibn Rushd’s response directs the demand to the guardian while discussing consequences connected with the child’s property.

questions.question: How does §42 treat puberty in relation to developed reason?
options: As a proof that every individual is intellectually identical
As proof that reason cannot be legally relevant
As a general practical sign rather than an instant physical creation of reason
As the only condition for every legal ruling
questions.explanation: Puberty serves as an administrable sign; it is not claimed to manufacture mature reason at that exact moment.

questions.question: What distinction is central to §47's account of an action performed under pressure?
options: The actor’s nationality and age
The type of legal school
The form of textual transmission
An initial external motive and an intention present when acting
questions.explanation: An initial extrinsic cause of action need not prevent a later intention of obedience at performance.

questions.question: A threatened person could physically refuse. Does that alone settle coercion for legal purposes?
options: Yes, because physical alternatives remove coercion
No, because threatened harm and the demanded act still matter
Yes, because intentions are legally irrelevant
No, because every pressure is equally decisive
questions.explanation: The availability of a physical alternative does not alone determine the legal classification of coercion.

questions.question: What is the key issue when ablution is a condition for prayer?
options: Whether a person can obtain the required condition
Whether there can be no condition for any act
Whether ablution is identical to praying
Whether a legal duty is solely a physical event
questions.explanation: §49 discusses conditions that can be obtained and rejects using failure to obtain them to erase a duty.

questions.question: What must not be inferred from a prayer obligation where ablution is obtainable?
options: The condition has an order relative to the act
The prayer may require preparatory action
The person may validly pray without the required purity
The inability to walk differs from obtainable purity
questions.explanation: Ibn Rushd’s point is not to authorise an invalid prayer but to show why an obtainable precondition cannot be bypassed.

questions.question: Which distinction is essential when an act must be made up later?
options: Translation versus transliteration
The later obligation versus blame for earlier nonperformance
Legal command versus prophetic action
Silence versus consensus
questions.explanation: §57 shows that a later duty of make-up performance does not in itself prove culpable earlier omission.

questions.question: A person performs an act described as commanded. Is that by itself enough to prove legal sufficiency?
options: Yes, every performed command is valid
Yes, provided the agent meant well
No, because acts do not have prescribed conditions
No, because the act’s prescribed conditions and character still matter
questions.explanation: §205 distinguishes the fact of a command from fulfilment of its legally sufficient prescribed form.

questions.question: What makes a legal concession different from an unrestricted permission?
options: It applies only to textual reports
It necessarily cancels all earlier law
It is tied to a relevant excuse or condition
It is reserved for jurists who memorise the Qurʾān
questions.explanation: §60 treats exceptional permissions in relation to the excuse or necessity that qualifies their scope.

questions.question: In §58’s discussion of travellers and fasting, what understood condition is significant?
options: That the traveller actually breaks the fast
That every traveller must never fast
That travel makes every duty disappear
That the traveller has no intention
questions.explanation: The dispute concerns whether make-up fasting is predicated on having broken the fast rather than travel alone.

questions.question: What must be distinguished from the Prophet’s own authority when later hearers receive a report?
options: The number of legal schools
The strength of evidence that the words were transmitted
The language of modern translations
The jurist’s preferred style
questions.explanation: §66 distinguishes direct hearing from mediated transmission; the latter raises an evidential question.

questions.question: Why can a solitary report warrant action without creating certainty about every individual report?
options: Because all solitary reports are equally reliable
Because certainty never matters
Because action on preponderant evidence can be authorised
Because the original speaker was not authoritative
questions.explanation: §81 defends legally warranted action on stronger probable evidence without identifying probability with certainty.

questions.question: What is 'retention' principally concerned with when assessing a transmitter?
options: Holding a legal office
Having the majority opinion
Belonging to a particular town
Accurately preserving what was heard
questions.explanation: Retention concerns reliability of memory and reproduction; probity concerns confidence in truthfulness.

questions.question: A trustworthy teacher firmly denies having said what a trustworthy student reports. What follows?
options: A real conflict may prevent action without proving either dishonest
The student is necessarily a liar
The report is automatically certain
The teacher’s probity becomes irrelevant
questions.explanation: §107 separates unresolved contradictory claims from an accusation of personal dishonesty.

questions.question: Which change most clearly requires checking whether an omitted context alters sense?
options: A report transmitted repeatedly
A completely new legal subject
An excerpt taken from a longer report
A jurist’s opinion without an isnād
questions.explanation: §110 permits abbreviation only when the remainder is independently intelligible and the omitted words do not distort it.

questions.question: Why might an addition to a jointly transmitted report be treated differently from a separate report?
options: Every addition is necessarily invented
Parallel transmissions provide relevant comparison evidence
All omission by others proves denial
A joint report cannot have variant wording
questions.explanation: The omitted detail in other witnesses is evidence to weigh, not an automatic refutation of the addition.

questions.question: Which is necessary to establish that one otherwise applicable ruling abrogated another?
options: An actual chronological basis for the later ruling
A younger narrator
A majority preference
A difference of wording alone
questions.explanation: §§115–129 distinguish proof of a later replacement from a merely apparent conflict or biographical inference.

questions.question: In §122, how might consensus relate to an abrogating revelation?
options: By enacting fresh revelation after the Prophet
By replacing the need for any evidence
By proving every consensus member’s infallibility
By evidencing an earlier abrogation rather than causing it
questions.explanation: The account allows consensus to disclose a prior abrogating warrant, not to create revelation anew.

questions.question: Why does 'most jurists agree' not by itself prove consensus?
options: Most jurists cannot discuss any ruling
Consensus has no relation to qualified jurists
The relevant agreement of all qualified participants has not been shown
Agreement cannot ever count as evidence
questions.explanation: §130’s definition requires an adequately established scope of agreement, not simply a majority tally.

questions.question: Which argument does §139 reject when genuine consensus has already been established?
options: It binds only when the entire agreeing generation has died
Agreement needs suitable participants
A claim of consensus needs evidence
Later disagreement differs from an original failure to agree
questions.explanation: Ibn Rushd rejects making the generation’s extinction a condition of an already genuine consensus.

questions.question: Who ordinarily must provide evidence when a new revealed obligation is claimed?
options: The person denying all duties
The person asserting the new obligation
The youngest witness
Every legal school simultaneously
questions.explanation: §141 places the burden of establishing a new revealed duty on its claimant.

questions.question: What changes when an already warranted ruling is said to have ceased?
options: The old ruling was never evidenced
All earlier proof becomes impossible
The situation is identical to positing a new duty
The question becomes whether contrary evidence defeats the established continuity
questions.explanation: §142 treats preservation of an established ruling as a different evidential starting point from original nonliability.

questions.question: A dictionary gives several meanings of ʿayn. What does that list by itself establish?
options: Which meaning Ibn Rushd necessarily intends
That every legal use shares all meanings
The available senses, not the intended sense in a given occurrence
That no contextual evidence can guide meaning
questions.explanation: §158’s multiple senses illustrate an ambiguity that is resolved by usage and contextual indications.

questions.question: Can specialised legal usage make a sense more apparent than its general lexical meaning?
options: Yes; §153 allows the legal sense to be apparent in its setting
No; dictionary order always decides
No; specialised usage has no semantic force
Yes; every technical expression is certainly unambiguous
questions.explanation: §153 distinguishes what is apparent in legal usage from a general-language sense; neither is an automatic universal rule.

questions.question: What is missing when someone offers a merely possible alternative to an apparent reading?
options: A longer quotation only
Any preference for the alternative grounded in evidence
A second language without context
A larger number of examples
questions.explanation: §§166–168 demand a relevant indication rather than a bare possibility of another meaning.

questions.question: How should the strength of an apparent meaning affect the warrant needed to interpret otherwise?
options: It never affects interpretation
Every metaphor requires the same proof
The interpreter may choose freely
A stronger apparent meaning requires correspondingly stronger countervailing evidence
questions.explanation: §167 links the burden on interpretation to how strongly the expression already indicates its apparent sense.

questions.question: Why is 'all kinds of water' unlike 'all senses of ʿayn'?
options: Water must be restricted to one well
The meaning of ʿayn is legally forbidden
Kinds of water share one sense; senses of ʿayn are distinct lexical meanings
A general term can never describe a kind
questions.explanation: §§169–177 distinguish coverage within one general meaning from selection among equivocal meanings.

questions.question: A generally worded answer addresses a question about one well. What alone does not restrict it?
options: The particular occasion that prompted the answer
The answer’s general wording
A relevant contextual indication
An explicit restriction in the answer
questions.explanation: §176 cautions against equating a particular occasion with a restriction on otherwise general wording.

questions.question: What makes an exception in §186 intelligible when the excepted term lies outside the named genus?
options: The named genus necessarily changes its literal identity
All grammatical exceptions are invalid
Only the first noun in the sentence matters
A broader understood communicative meaning can govern the exception
questions.explanation: The ‘man … except a woman’ example invokes a contextual denial of anyone, not reclassification of a woman as a man.

questions.question: For an exception following multiple clauses, what is relevant to its scope?
options: Its distance from the beginning alone
Whether the clauses express one meaning or several, and the evidence
Whether the shortest clause is first
Whether all the clauses are equally long
questions.explanation: §187 distinguishes shared meanings from separate meanings and may require further evidence of scope.

questions.question: In 'Ask the village,' what is supplied by understood meaning?
options: The village’s inhabitants
A different legal source
The name of a particular jurist
A new command invented by the interpreter
questions.explanation: §194 treats inhabitants as understood from the communicative setting without their being named.

questions.question: Does an unstated element automatically make the intended meaning uncertain?
options: Yes, absence of wording prevents any certainty
Yes, all implied meaning is mere conjecture
No, contextual evidence can establish the omitted element decisively
No, because every possible omission has equal authority
questions.explanation: §§193–194 distinguish linguistic omission from the degree of certainty warranted by context.

questions.question: What is still open after recognising an imperative form?
options: Whether it occurs in Arabic
Its legal force, timing and requirement of repetition
Whether a transmitter exists
Whether all legal duties were abrogated
questions.explanation: §§197–203 treat force, timing and repetition as distinct issues rather than a single conclusion from the form.

questions.question: Why can a command to hunt after leaving consecration indicate permission?
options: Every imperative always means permission
Hunting cannot be forbidden in any situation
The command is itself a repeated obligation
It can remove a previous restriction without imposing a new duty to hunt
questions.explanation: §203 relates the command to an earlier restriction and its removal; this reading is context-dependent.

questions.question: In §212's extension from silver to gold vessels, what broader meaning is proposed?
options: Purity of metals
A change of date
Extravagance as an intended relevant universal
Agreement of all jurists
questions.explanation: The extension is based on an alleged wider intended meaning of extravagance rather than metal resemblance alone.

questions.question: What two warrants are required before extending the ruling to a new case?
options: That the universal meaning is intended and that the new case falls under it
That both cases have identical names and prices
That the later case has more narrators
That both cases are found in one dictionary
questions.explanation: §§210–213 separate establishing the law’s intended universal from establishing the new case as one of its instances.

questions.question: Why can a stronger unmentioned case inherit a prohibition of a lesser harm?
options: Every larger object receives a stricter ruling
The prohibited relevant meaning is even more present in it
All unstated meanings are equal
The new case has a longer description
questions.explanation: §215’s example of stronger mistreatment depends on intensified disrespect, not arbitrary material magnitude.

questions.question: Why is a merely suggested resemblance in §218 insufficient for a decisive extension?
options: It is already a demonstration
It always counts as consensus
It replaces the original text
The operative ground has not been securely identified
questions.explanation: A resemblance is not yet an adequately justified legal ground for transferring the ruling.

questions.question: What must be established beyond the bare observation of a Prophetic action?
options: Whether the action occurred in daylight
Whether later jurists preferred it
What legal significance it had in its context
Whether an exact English translation exists
questions.explanation: §228 distinguishes actions that explain obligations or recommendations, actions particular to the Prophet, and uncertain cases.

questions.question: What makes an appeal to tacit approval evidentially relevant under §227?
options: Reliable knowledge that the act occurred in his presence, was seen, and was approved
A later author’s silence in a separate book
The absence of every contrary opinion
The fact that the action was physically possible
questions.explanation: §227 requires sufficiently established presence, observation and approval, with attention to the circumstances.

questions.question: Which qualification can be relaxed without removing the need for understanding evidence?
options: The ability to evaluate relevant indications
Memorising every relevant text rather than knowing how to find it
Knowing the issue’s legal conditions
Using appropriate methods of inquiry
questions.explanation: §232 distinguishes ready access to passages from memorisation while preserving substantive juristic competence.

questions.question: When may inquiry be confined to one question under §236?
options: Whenever the issue sounds simple
When a scholar memorises a single report
When some other jurist agrees
When the person has sufficient knowledge for that specific question
questions.explanation: Partial competence must still be sufficient for the whole question under investigation.

questions.question: Which two questions does the discussion of excused error keep distinct?
options: Which school is oldest and which is largest
Which book came first and which second
Whether a judgement is true and whether its author is culpable
Whether every report was memorised and translated
questions.explanation: §§237–245 distinguish correct legal judgement from personal blame for a mistaken effort.

questions.question: What is the proper implication of pardon for an inadvertent mistake?
options: The agent may be excused without making the mistaken judgement true
All opposed conclusions become simultaneously true
Every careless judgement is excused
No jurist can ever be mistaken
questions.explanation: §243’s appeal to inadvertence mitigates culpability without changing the truth value of a conclusion.

questions.question: Why does Ibn Rushd question automatic adoption of the strictest rule when proofs conflict?
options: Every disputed ruling is void
A stricter requirement can itself add an unwarranted duty
The strictest option always creates consensus
Differences in evidence cannot affect action
questions.explanation: §246 notes that automatic caution may impose obligations without the proof required for doing so.

questions.question: What does the existence of two juristic opinions prove about their evidential strength?
options: That both are certain
That choice is always unrestricted
That neither may be followed
Nothing by itself; one may be better supported than the other
questions.explanation: §257 concerns weighing actual evidence rather than treating a plurality of opinions as equally strong.

questions.question: Which community arrangement does §250 treat as necessary and sustainable?
options: Every person is a full-time jurist
No one learns the legal methods
Some acquire expertise while others legitimately rely on them
Only inherited prestige decides every case
questions.explanation: Ibn Rushd criticises universal specialisation and universal ignorance and defends divided but real competence.

questions.question: Why is legitimate reliance more than attaching oneself to a famous jurist’s name?
options: It depends on actual qualified inquiry, preservation and teaching
Names alone make every new question settled
It means no community must investigate new questions
It is unrelated to the preservation of legal knowledge
questions.explanation: §§249–255 describe reliance as a relation to substantive scholarly work, not a substitute for it.
